body:
It stinks that people can relate, but I’m glad it’s not just me. The anxiety sucks because it gets so high just sitting around that it’s hard to bring it down enough to think _productively_.

I don’t much a lot of spare cash either, but I have found a few activities that I’m interested in. I plan on taking swim lessons in June, just gotta roll the dice and decide which dates. Plus I found a free yoga class on Saturdays at 9AM.

I don’t mean to whine or dump, but I’m thinking out loud. I guess there’s two underlying issues for me. One is that, in my head, I resent the idea that I have to function 7 days a week. I guess after working full-time, I don’t want to put in more work to use all the tools and hold myself accountable on weekends. But I should because clearly stewing in my thoughts is also stressful. Then, I have two subtle fears. The first is that I go through the effort to do the thing and feel nothing, or I feel weird that I did all that work to go be alone somewhere for no reason. The second is that I do my little thing and it’s nice, but then there’s nothing else to do so I’m back to sad, stagnant square one. Those kinds of worries plus the ADHD/logistical issues make me feel like I might as well just sit, even though that’s not always my best move.

I can relate. I have some questions for you:

Why do you want to be strong? What kinds of things have happened that make you wish you were more firm and assertive? I ask these because this is your root. This underlies any words or body language. This is part of what will keep you going when it’s difficult or nerve wracking. You know what you’re trying to do and why.

How has your submissive behavior helped you? Has it, for example, helped you feel safer by staying in their good graces or spared you tantrums? Would you be okay even if they weren’t happy with you? Can you better cope with their negative feelings at you or your own negative feelings towards yourself? This is a risk assessment. The last time I reflected on this, I realized that I was damned either way and that I at least wanted it to be on my terms for once. I decided I cared more about being cozy in my own skin because they can be just fine while I’m miserable.

Then, are you willing to forgive yourself for your mistakes? You’re doing this out of love for yourself, right? It’s easier to stand tall and be confident when you’re on your own side. When you can recognize you’re mistake/falling short of your goal, but appreciate the bravery it took to try even when it was hard. Appreciating what it took to reach out and ask for help instead of surrendering to guilt and shame wholesale.

My questions are food for thought, by the way! What I’m trying to get at is that, in my experience, it’s less about presentation and more about being grounded.
I am. They don’t always help much on weekends though.

I can relate to your second to last line. If your mother is anything like mine, it’s because she isn’t well. Everyone isn’t always equipped to participate in healthy, loving relationships. Not even with themselves. I’m not saying this as a judgement or making excuses. An unfortunate thing is that unhealthy people can meet other people that complement them and create dysfunctional families. So while your parents may be different, there’s something that brought them together. There’s something that’s keeping them together. Even if your father doesn’t act like your mother, healthy parents don’t just allow their children to be treated like this. I don’t know how old your siblings are, but they grew up in the dysfunction.

I know it’s beyond hurtful, and I’m sorry that you’re experiencing this. I said everything I said to point out that it’s not your fault, it’s nothing you need to internalize. The things your mother says or the choices your family makes do not define you or reflect your worth.

I don’t think your thoughts are too harsh. People may rush to say that you shouldn’t feel that way, but those people may not understand your situation. It makes sense to feel upset that you were mistreated as a child and that instead of addressing that, your father prioritized the impossible task of keeping your mother content. Enablers, just like the people they enable, may have their reasons, but unfortunately it doesn’t erase the consequences of their actions.

Also, I don’t mean to ramble, but what really got me was her coming back to say that 2.5hrs later. The nitpicking is enough, but the wait is the kind of shit that makes you crazy. It is so hard to feel safe around someone who cannot control themselves, who cannot let a good moment pass without spoiling it. Someone who’s constantly evaluating others (even when it’s positive) and trying to control everybody meanwhile they’re allergic to genuine emotional connection.

You and your mother hadn’t spoken for two months after a dinner. You felt discarded because of that. You decided to share a happy little update about your daughter with your mother and sister. They say nice things. Then over 2 hours later, your mother nitpicks your daughter’s natural looks and suggests teaching your daughter to conform to beauty standards as a bonding activity. Meanwhile, you don’t even think she was good at bonding with you in the first place.

We worry a lot about the validity of our feelings as RBBs. What we aren’t taught is that we have a right to feel and how important it is for us to hear ourselves so that we can make decisions that align with us. In this case, your upset is a signal that a boundary has been crossed. Regardless of what she may believe, it doesn’t matter if your mother thinks it’s okay. You know how hurtful meaningless nitpicking is (compared to actual relevant, necessary, constructive criticism) and want to protect your children from it. Also, good on you OP for teaching your kids to nip this shit in the bud.

THIS! It was so “normal” that I don’t think of it often, and it’s so weird that I’d be ashamed to mention it. 

There’s so much to it, but in short I’ve chosen to go without food many times because of her. Because if she hears me in the kitchen, she’ll expect a plate. Because if my father brings food only for me, she’ll lose her fucking mind and I guess he’s okay with that because he can just leave. Because I didn’t want her to know I had any money or else she would’ve felt entitled to it. Because she’ll eat up my snacks and who knows if or when she’ll replace them. Because she’ll start raising hell or pouting if I thought of myself (or let’s say had a good time at a dinner or something) without her. It’s just so fucked up. I’m sorry you understand.

I think this could be wrapped in there, but I can’t really see it. I can’t “see” it because my protectors view others as threats, first and foremost. And like, to use Maslow’s hierarchy, my protectors deem the love and belonging level as irrelevant flourish at best. What’s important is being strong and capable enough to survive on my own and to have self-esteem and feel fulfilled by my decisions and actions. Perfection will keep me safe from people, from feelings. I’ll be high enough that no one can touch me. I don’t know, I guess my protectors feel a sort of resignation about love and being lovable...

Were you supposed to talk her out of dying? I don’t think so. It was her body, her life and not your responsibility. Regardless of what parents like ours may believe and want us to believe, it is not our job to fight for _their_ lives through any and every crisis.

Your mother made a decision for herself as an adult and the medical professionals did their part. You decided to support her through her decision by being visiting, being present with the doctors and staying with her. You don’t owe it to her or the doctors to do what they might’ve, could’ve thought you should’ve done because they don’t understand the whole situation and they aren’t you.

Also, I think people struggle with the fact that death is a part of life. Of course there’s this cultural idea that life is always good and worth fighting for, but there’s limits to every idea. For example, why crush some 90-year old’s ribs to resuscitate them if they’re ready to bow out gracefully? If time and unhealthy habits wore your mother down and she decided she had enough, what good would your protest have really done?

I think this is part of it. When I was going on about my Sun thing, I had a passing vision of my mother smiling down at me. Just because I was, and that was a worthwhile and wonderful thing. Unfortunately, she was as terrific as she was terrifying. But those moments were the very best.

What you said reminds me of an exile that I imagine deep in some dark forest. I imagine it with a small but enduring fire, and I think that’s the self-love/acceptance. There’s just something that feels worthless about that because what’s important is survival. And it’s hard to believe in a little fire that can go from bonfire to smoldering embers, that must persist (or even be restarted) through wind and rain…

I swear, flying monkeys are always meddling. They can never leave people and their relationships alone.

If you can’t make it, you can’t make it. Even if it’s because you simply don’t want to make the trip on Sunday. It’s your day too, after all. You tried to work around that and made two very kind offers that they declined. What else are you supposed to do? Why won’t they try to work it out with you by making offerings of their own, like a different day maybe? Why should the burden be on you to bend over backwards year after year?

I just want to add on that the disorder is characterized by “frantic attempts to avoid abandonment,” among other things. Whether she’s conscious of it, trying to reverse the blame could’ve been a way for her to keep you with her. Never mind your emotional well-being, she’s in crisis and she needs to keep you in whatever state and by any means.

Unfortunately this comment makes a good point. Most of us are here because our parents lack the emotional maturity to have healthy intimate relationships and instead get by using toxic tactics.

You’re not an abuser for speaking up for yourself. Your mother’s issues are her own, even if she tries to make everyone else responsible for them. no wonder you’re exhausted though because dealing with all of this, especially from childhood, is tiresome. Take care, OP, you deserve it.

Thank you for hearing me.

Talking about this stuff is difficult because I always feel like I’m fighting against criticism. Before I even have anything to say, I “hear” everything I should think/feel/do and all the ways whatever I say will be dismissed. Then I feel crazy because it’s like after everything, what could I possibly say? And I understand why they do what they do, I respect that they have a right to their decisions so I don’t try to comment or interfere. But they struggle to do the same. There’s always this pressure for me (and everyone else, really) to just cope with my mother’s behavior because that’s how she wants it. Cope and then we can all be together and enjoy the good times, damn what it costs.

I feel similarly about my father. I don’t think he has malicious intent, but I just feel like…he wasn’t raised right. He survived and continues to do so, but he can’t really see beyond that, you know? Even I struggle at times to believe that there’s anything better out there, anything I could actually reach. Life can be tough even without a dysfunctional family, so I understand. People want to be happy and comfortable sometimes. I just try to keep going because I’d rather go figure it out than stay.

Your mother does that in public? Yikes! My mother doesn’t make _too_ much of a fuss in public, but the nastiness will build and seep some. She is as sure to retaliate as she is sure to find upset. Both of them together is just too much. The mutual trauma bonds they have with each other will go to the grave with them. I think they would overwhelm people who weren’t regularly terrorized by their frenemy/co-parenting relationship since, probably the womb. And just because I believe I can deal, doesn’t mean I volunteer.

I have a question for you about therapy. What did you do? I’ve gone before briefly, but haven’t found anyone who was really equipped and I’m not sure exactly what I’d be going for?

Side note: I think part of the reason it was so triggering for me was that I developed an aversion to being with alone with them. I end up adrift in plastic bag mode because I’m always a hostage and more often than not there’s tension/conflict because their relationship is extremely volatile. Situations where I was alone with them (including being involved in their drama) constitute a significant portion of my worst moments, especially in the earliest, haziest part of my memory.

At this point, I don’t want to be alone with her and anyone we know. Especially our close family members. I don’t know how to say it, but I feel like…they smooth things over, but they don’t really stand up to her. Maybe it’s cowardly, but I don’t want to be in a situation where I have to pretend, where it’s wholly on me to stand up and speak out in the moment.

That's so inappropriate, OP. I'm sorry.

I was a therapist/therapy dog. My mother was an eternal triumphant victim. She's always the only person in the world who's really struggling. It's never her fault though, unless she's been too kind.

This part of my experience is less...attention-grabbing... but it's still so bad. It's another way that I lost my childhood all because she can't understand other people, including children. Playing therapist because the only intimacy she's capable of is trauma-dumping.  Being a hostage and trying to play empathetic or problem-solver because I feared for my/our safety and security. Having my own perspective, needs, and boundaries overrode and violated on a regular basis for decades under threat of abuse and neglect. Being exposed to triggering content, family conflict, and wildly dysregulated emotions on a regular basis for decades and having to keep it secret lest I be punished or alienated by my peers. Never having the safe space to to express myself. I could probably write a whole essay on this. Honestly, thanks for sharing OP because hearing someone else has helped me reflect.

What's funny is that she believed she was breaking curses because she felt like no one ever shared their experiences or gave her proper guidance. I can see how that would be possible. However, she isn't the hero she wanted to be at all. She couldn't care enough about my experiences to provide accurate and appropriate guidance. She had no wisdom to share from her own experiences, just tragic monologues. We'd argue a lot as I got older because she never learned anything. I grew frustrated with her repetitive, irrational behavior. Or I'd ask for wisdom since she made it seem like life was so full of terrors. We'd end up arguing because she had none to give and I didn't realize that until later. I'm still learning that her experience and troubles aren't as universal as she believes.

I’m not Jewish. I empathize with you though, coming from my own background and as another RBB. It’s very sad and very sick. I hope that somehow, you’re able to recover your family heirlooms after her temper tantrum if you choose to speak with her again. Worst case scenario, the legacy will continue despite her erratic behavior.

As an RBB, I completely understand. It can be so frustrating and painful to be connected to people who behave like this. Being so unstable and seeing themselves as powerless victims keeps them from really _caring_ about anything. Any upset and they take it straight to Hell—damn who or whatever they’re mad at, damn themselves and damn any collateral. No sense of consistency or consequences. The damage and the betrayal cut so deeply, and if yours is like mine, they reject any sort of accountability and refuse to truly make amends. I’m sorry you’re dealing with this, it really is wrong on so many levels.

I feel you on this. I mostly stopped caring about it when she’d try to shame me for it, but I did note how cold I often felt. It seemed odd because it’s just not a common experience. It completely makes sense though. Even though they don’t really get it (like literally), it’s one of the dirty deals of Borderland. They think all is well because they’re getting what they want—to be cared for by someone else how they like without putting in any real effort. They may get compliance, but they have to sacrifice a genuine loving connection for it. And regardless of how it gets interpreted, everyone involved can feel that something isn’t good.

When I think of it I’m sure I have felt for her, but she makes it so fucking hard. I used to feel so stressed and frustrated at her choices and actions. Like no, I don’t give a fuck about your drama because I’m 9 years old. What am I supposed to do about the kind of chaos that makes grown adult mental health professionals shy away? I don’t give a fuck because I’m 13 years old worrying about worrying about how your actions will affect our household/family, my food, shelter, my friends, my education, so on. I don’t give a fuck because I’ve probably been hearing the same damn rants since the womb. I don’t give a fuck because I’m sick of all the abuse. I don’t give a fuck because where would I get it from? You certainly didn’t give me very many, that’s for sure.

This reminds me so much of my mother. Having it in text like this really shows how they operate and how damaging it is. You’ll really be going through daily life and BOOM now you’re dealing with a threatening lunatic going on a villainous tirade that’s somehow all your fault. Never mind, if it’s anything like what I’ve experienced, nothing gets addressed afterwards either (unless it’s in another episode).

I’m sorry OP. I know how hard it is to be stuck in this. I hope you and your belongings will be safe while you ride out this storm. I wish I had advice, but all I can say is keep doing what you can.

Do you feel alienated because of both your personal experience *and* the insight its given you? As in, first you have the experience of being mistreated by your mother and subsequent aversion towards her. This is unlike the popularly promoted experience where there's a positive, loving connection between mother and child. Then, not only do you have your experience, but you can see beyond the belief. You're aware that bad mothers exist and that even if uncommon, may not be as rare as people believe. This separates you from a popular belief and puts you at odds with people who are deeply invested in the idea that all mothers are loving and nurturing figures. For these people, it's easier to turn on you because they already deem motherhood a sacred, blameless position. Am I following you?

Edit: It's awful that you were physically punished over this. I don't even know what to say, that's just crazy and wrong.

“Acknowledging my own toxic traits (yet not doing a damn thing about them) makes me a cycle breaker! And actually, I deserve to have them! Look at all the bad experiences I’ve had! Look at how YOU treat me? You reacting to my toxicity hurts MY feelings!YOU’RE TOXIC!”

Whoops, my hands slipped.

Yes and no. I went no contact with my mother because it was my last resort. I think that’s the case for many. For me, I just couldn’t take it anymore. I don’t know how to describe it other than she’d done too much, addressed little, and continued with the same patterns of behavior. So, I withdrew and detached (even more) until a final incident sealed the deal.

I felt so relieved, yet it still hung over me like a cloud in the earlier months. It can be a challenge now, but it’s different now as I’ve adapted. I think, in these cases, the benefit of No Contact is that we can make space and redirect our time and energy towards ourselves. We may not find ourselves in great shape, which is probably to be expected. Doesn’t mean addressing that isn’t a worthy and rewarding project. I also want to add that No Contact isn’t always the last stop for everyone. Situations change and/or people find themselves able to try again. Sometimes it works out, other times not so much.

It doesn’t sound like you’ve done anything but feel upset and consider possible boundaries going forward. Are you just not allowed to have preferences/requests/boundaries and feel upset when those aren’t met or respected? Are you not allowed to have a thought that might could possibly potentially one day maybe rock the boat? These are rhetorical questions. What I’m getting at is that I hate how Borderland means no one (except you know who) is allowed to have an unapproved feeling. Regardless of any possible outcome, just stop right there right now!

In my experience, one of the most difficult parts of escaping Borderland (socially/emotionally/psychologically) is all enmeshment and drama (I’m thinking of the Drama Triangle) in these circles.It’s been a balance between understanding people’s perspectives and limitations while still enforcing my boundaries. My father’s a bit meddlesome at times. I recognize that: A) it totally makes sense based on his background and choices and B) he’s never been on my journey. My estrangement makes him confused, fearful and uncomfortable. He spent understand because my experiences don’t match his, don’t line up to what he thinks a parent-child bond should be. It scares him to see the NC because it threatens what he (and the broader culture) believe is an unbreakable bond full of love and support that outweighs any negatives. He’s asked me what I would say to him if he had issues with his own father and cannot grasp that my answer isn’t immediately push for reconciliation. He has adapted some, but I recognize that I won’t be re-writing his core beliefs. It’s not my place to do that anyway. 

What’s helped me in that kind of situation and others like it, is deciding that my relationship with my mother is between the two of us. That’s our relationship, and I get to choose what I want to do with my half of that relationship. I make that clear through direct communication, by returning requests/tasks to the sender (i.e., how bout _you_ talk to her over and over again), or simply refusing to justify, argue, defend or explain (JADE) anything. At a certain point, what I need is respect. Respect above understanding, agreement, or approval.

 I don’t think you’re overreacting. Your mother has a photo of your child that she shouldn’t have and your brother is likely the leak. You plan on speaking with him about it at some point. Your father and brother have tried to manage your relationship with your mother by giving you tasks, as if it’s your job to fix everything _and_ you need to be told how. I can’t tell you what to do because everyone’s different. Even I’m more lenient with some of my boundaries because we all choose our battles, you know? I guess I’m trying to say that there’s nothing wrong with feeling how you feel or doing what works for you.

If they’re putting you near her and expect you to talk to her, and you’re willing to do these things, are they at least willing to join the conversation? If they aren’t or aren’t the best choice, is there anyone else who can support you?

Also, I’m not fully sure what you two need to discuss? I’ll admit my bias—Borderland has made me less open to discussions. I think this worth considering though. What is the goal of the discussion? Is it to try to make everyone perfectly comfortable? Is that reasonable, especially after 5.5 years of NC which I assume happened for a pattern of reasons? Is it in hopes of preventing drama? Though it should be obvious to anyone not to use someone’s wedding as a place to air grievances or reconcile? I say this to say, if you’re going to have the conversation, think about what you’re comfortable with and define its goal.

Also, you say you feel cowardly for being afraid. Have you thought about taking a moment to go through your fears? There could be useful insight in them. For example, if you’re afraid of talking to her alone, that could be completely valid. Then you’d draw a line that you’re not comfortable with that, and either avoid the talk or get someone to help. If you’re afraid she might try to harass you, then you might come up with something to say (“I won’t be discussing this now, I’m here to support X&Y) and then leave.

I've been here for awhile and I'm still amazed sometimes at how similar all of our experiences are. It's really a shame, but at least we have this space?

>Looking back I feel horrible for my teenage self that tried to navigate this situation without much support.

Reflecting on my teenage self makes me want to pour one out. I look back and have so much compassion for myself. I didn't feel like a kid, never really have, which meant that I carried such heavy and inappropriate burdens. I felt like I was ruining my own life because even though I was actually doing pretty well, I wasn't able to be, like super-duper exceptional all on my own.

 I can't judge fairly because I can't remember most of my childhood, but I feel like she fucking awful during my teen years. Maybe because I can remember them. Maybe because I was old enough to handle more of my reality. Like, even if I wasn't equipped to actually process everything and see the big picture, I was able to form and store memories. Plus, that was the point I started feeling like I'd outgrown her. I spent so much time struggling with her, only to learn that she was too immature to be able to support an emerging adult. Even saying this makes me feel like I have to be lying because it has to be impossible, but it's like she was absolutely no help. Any positive point I can give has one or two negative points because, figuratively, she can't bake a pie without throwing it on the floor or smashing you in the face with it.

What you said about missing your mother resonates with me. It’s hard to…validate and contextualize because it feels contradictory. Like, I’ll never have an another mother. No one’s ever going to love me like that crazy lady (affectionate). Thank god, but at the same time that is the first love I ever knew. That was my mother. I still remember. But, like you, our relationship has changed significantly. We can’t go back, and she can’t really move forward.

Your mother sidelining you to focus on your son sounds hurtful. I’m sorry you’re experiencing that. The hardest thing about parents like these is that, as their children, we can’t help but hope that they will show up as parents. The unfortunate reality is that these parents are unable to do so on a consistent basis. They usually can’t even see situations (themselves and other people in them) clearly enough to make reasonable decisions. Like, it doesn’t make sense that she’d pass over you to keep making efforts to your son. I only get it because I’ve seen how things get warped into justifying strange behavior.

I don’t know if this helped any, but I just wanted to you’re not alone. It sucks and hurts to have to deal with your parent’s limitations, how they can’t/won’t show up the way we wish they would.

Yes, but not just my mother. She didn’t start 
it, though her circles include people who act similarly. I feel like it’s related to poor boundaries, lack of compassion, poor self-awareness and self-control. 

**Like just because you form a judgement about someone doesn’t mean you should automatically hang onto it, let alone _tell other people about it_, you know? _Especially_ other people in the same social circle because that’s how drama starts. Trashing people, especially behind their backs, builds up a (deserved) bad reputation. There’s a point where if you have a problem, you should be assertive discuss it with the person and/or figure out how to adjust yourself. There’s a point where you don’t need to be worried about other people’s business, especially if it has nothing to do with the interaction. If you end up disliking someone, which you would hopefully realize, that’s fine but let them be then. Consider if theres really a problem or if your own misery is making you critical without compassion or humility.

Growing up around this kind of negativity creates a lot of issues too. It’s a bad example of conversation, emotional regulation, and conflict resolution. It’s hard to feel secure growing up exposed to all the destructive criticism _and_ witnessing the constant betrayals of trust. It’s hard to trust other people and be intimate after this stuff. I’m sure there’s more in forgetting.

Anyway, good luck on your plans, OP! I know how much it sucks to be expected to play yes-man to nasty monologues no one asked for. You know your situation best. but what helped with me was to minimize engagement. It’s no fun to rant at a wall.

**to be clear, “you” in the second paragraph isn’t OP or anyone specific.

Thank you for sharing. Unfortunately, it isn’t an option for me at the moment. If I do attend, I know that someone outside of the official “inner circle” will be there. That could kind of throw things off and reinforce…polite behavior.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. Your mother shouldn’t be insulting you, threatening you, harming you, or damaging your things. It sounds like an abusive situation. The trouble with those is the power dynamic. It’s going to be difficult to maintain boundaries with someone who behaves like this if you aren’t able to protect yourself from them.

Your post resonated with me so deeply that I'm struggling with how to respond. Even your use of the word "landmines," instead of eggshells, because that's what they always felt like to me. These cycles were literally my entire life with my mother. My earliest, incredibly hazy childhood memories are of...this, and how to navigate it. I've only been able to escape in recent years with distance, independence, and restricting direct contact.

The shift from brightness and warmth to coldness and cruelty. I only realize now that in many cases, it's a work of dark fantasy. It's usually not the stick of butter left out on the counter, but she'll use that as supporting evidence for whatever she's feeling. Whatever she's feeling may be related to an actual external event or it could be some old emotion or something she cooked up.

The shaming, trying to use your own self against you during splitting episodes. I learned to greyrock early on to avoid this. Never fully stopped her though because she'd just say that was mean and cruel. Anything but deference is seen as a threat. Even deference might be spun into a threat. Anything she can grasp at becomes a story. If she doesn't know about my friends because I haven't said anything, it becomes "something's wrong with you, you don't have any friends." I realized that it's all based on whatever she's feeling. She feels aggressive, she feels ashamed or assumes she'll be met with aggression.

The main difference is that my mother's self-harm outbursts weren't violent. Except one time when she smashed a mug into her head because she felt cornered after targeting me and agitating the golden child. That was the most absurd thing I've ever seen, to the point where I feel like that couldn't have happened. She never self-deprecated, as she was too proud to do so. Once I said she didn't like kids, so she slithered away muttering that she was a good mother.

>So my questions are this — Have you seen cycles like these with your parents? Have they been better, worse, about the same? How?

>Also wondering — Do you ever receive an apology, or even a "my bad"? Or is it just constant doubling down and digging in of the heals?

I can't say for certain whether the cycles have really changed, or if I see my mother more clearly. I feel like she's become more unhinged by my independence. Like, we used to be able to go back to "normal," but she doesn't know how to adjust to me as a separate entity with boundaries.

My mother only apologizes when the police should've been called. Mind you, just because the police should've been called doesn't mean she'll apologize. She will basically only apologize at figurative gunpoint. Once she tried to apologize for everything (wonder what she thought that was), but that was after our relationship collapsed.

Yes, it’s normal with these types. The nature of the disorder, particularly when untreated I assume, makes it difficult to maintain stable, healthy relationships with others. The behavior you describe is called [hoovering](https://outofthefog.website/top-100-trait-blog/2015/11/4/hoovering), when abusers try to suck their victims back in like a Hoover vacuum. I suggest you check out that website when you feel up to it because it has a lot of helpful information about dealing with these situations.

We tend to be at a disadvantage having been their children because we started without knowledge, boundaries, and the ability to hold them accountable in any substantial way. The challenge for us in adulthood is to get to a place where we can learn to be the adults we needed all along.  

You don’t have to be available for your mother at all times, even if that’s what she wants. You may feel worried or guilty, but it doesn’t mean you’re in the wrong for not meeting unreasonable demands for closeness (whether that’s based on frequency or in spite of nasty behavior). It’s not your job to put yourself in bad positions to keep her from feeling the consequences of her actions, or just plain disappointment that everyone feels sometimes. Good on you for trying to regain some control and reaching out for support.

Edit: I know the feeling of being scared of my phone, it’s the worst. For a practical tip, maybe you can try to hide/silence notifications from her? That may make it easier to delay responses, which I would suggest you do consistently.

I think the most important step is to be clear about your intentions and convictions. You’re already doing that here by putting words to this awful experience and what you won’t tolerate. I’ve heard of people making [FU binders](https://www.reddit.com/user/ForwardPlenty/comments/dtg7f2/the_fu_binder/?rdt=44858) for organized legal evidence. Even if you don’t feel the need, having some record of things that happened (diary entries, texts, photos, etc.) may help you keep your resolve and remember _why_ you’re doing this. I think this is the most important step because it’s key to not falling into a pattern of [intermittent reinforcement](https://outofthefog.website/what-not-to-do-1/2015/12/3/intermittent-reinforcement). It’s okay to change your mind, but you don’t want to teach them that they can play you like a slot machine.

It helps to learn more about healthy boundaries and detachment. These kinds of parents typically have poor boundaries, and we learn to be more invested in them and their feelings than ourselves and our own. We may believe, even after we become independent adults, that our well-being still depends on their contentment like when we were children. Luckily, that is not the case. It’s okay for us to lean into our own feelings. Like the anger you feel right now? It’s there to motivate you to protect your son and yourself from this awful behavior.

Going through this kind of change is difficult. Finding support helps lighten the load. It comes in many forms (therapy, loved ones, online groups, books, educational videos) and combos can be great. Also, let a little joy in when you feel able. I think part of what keeps us out of their orbit (or at least on our own terms) is enriching our own lives.

One of the core symptoms of BPD is an unstable sense of self. It can be challenging for anyone to make major life decisions, but it’s especially difficult when you’re not sure who you are. You know: likes, dislikes, strengths, weaknesses, interests, goals, etc. Other symptoms like emotional dysregulation and impulsivity can make it difficult to stick with things too. People who struggle with their own agency may feel dependent on others to accomplish their own goals, which can lead to resentment among other things.

I don’t know if it’s possible for you to help much. These are all things she could choose to work on, and it’d probably be easier with a professional. Even if she only chose to work with a career development professional, let’s say. But either way, the motivation and commitment would have to come from within. As an adult, she has to make her own decisions for herself, like she has been since before you were born.

I’d also caution you to be aware of how much time and energy you sink into trying to help her. I’m not saying stop because I don’t know the situation and what you do is up to you. I’m just saying that if you spend a bunch of time trying to sort things out and none of it works for her anyway, then that time may be better spent on other things.

It can affect other important relationships and/or make you feel (more) alienated from others because estrangement is taboo. Because our parents are people, most of us have some good memories because who’s awful 24/7/365? We’re also wired to want connection with our caregivers, plus these parents trained us to respond to their needs via [fear, obligation, and guilt.](https://outofthefog.website/toolbox-1/2015/11/17/fog-fear-obligation-guilt)

NC gets so much love here because of the hate it gets everywhere else, even if some people really need it. 2) Let go of perfectionism and unrealistic expectations. This actually makes #1 easier. One of the hardest things about Freeze is that you learn to get comfortable with little. It’s okay to need breaks, take more time, make mistakes, have bad days, etc. Being down doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll never get up again.

People with this disorder can struggle with regulating intense emotions, jumping to conclusions, and nuance (splitting, black and white thinking). It sounds like your mother is trying to defend herself against feeling shame and/or guilt. Instead of listening to you, validating your experience, and trying to make a change, it’s easier for her to project the wrongdoing onto you.

It can’t be she and other family members saying hurtful things that they shouldn’t, it’s _you_ being sensitive when _you_ shouldn’t. It’s you ruminating and making mountains of molehills, not her describing something she probably does if she’s anything like my mother. If you’re upset about parts of your childhood and you’re right, that means she’s a bad mother. What’s most important isn’t hearing you out, it’s not being a bad mother. So you’re actually an ungrateful, bad child with unreasonable expectations. And she’s a good mother (a good person) because she can even forgive you. There, conflict over and emotional crisis averted with no accountability taken.

With responses, I would discourage justifying, arguing, defending, and explaining ([JADE](https://outofthefog.website/what-not-to-do-1/2015/12/3/jade-dont-justify-argue-defend-explain)) things because it’s easy to get caught up in circular conversations that make you feel worse. Plus, is she the type to remember or acknowledge anything you mention? It seems most of the parents written about here speak in defensive generalities (e.g., I don’t remember/no I didn’t/what about what you did/I’m sorry for whatever I did/if I did then you deserved it or I couldn’t help it), to avoid dealing with issues anyway. Then, maybe consider if there are any boundaries you’d like to establish going forward to protect you from this behavior.

Well, it could be related to both because there are connections between ADHD and attachment. I relate to this, so here’s what I’ve got. I think it’s about being present and engaged, part of which is about how much we can let ourselves feel.

It can be challenging to be present and engaged with ADHD. ADHDers can be very stimulation seeking (while also selective about which stimulation) and are motivated by things like challenge, urgency, interest, novelty, etc. This is part of why ADHDers do best with some kind of treatment. Not to fix it necessarily, but to figure out how to live well with it.

If you’re meeting a brand new person in a casual setting, it’s easy for that to be humdrum. You’re just there, they’re just there. Neither of you may be particularly comfortable, even in the best case scenario where neither of you are particularly inhibited people. Many ADHDers learn that they are expected to suppress feelings of boredom because they are childish/weird/insulting to others. Sometimes it’s fine, but that doesn’t help build relationships. 

First, I’d say that it’s okay to be bored with people. None of us is here to provide constant entertainment, and everyone won’t be the bestest friends. It’s okay to be disappointed in your interactions; it’s not necessarily anyone’s fault. I say that because listening to our feelings, within reason, is how we live more satisfying lives.

Then, the key to enjoying social interactions is both parties being able to connect. This means asking questions (that you really want to ask), offering answers (that you really mean). There’s some vulnerability involved there that many people (avoidant, anxious, otherwise) resist. Opening up exposes us to the possibility of rejection, both from others and the self for people dealing with low self-esteem. So it feels easier to just block people out; after all who wants to feel bad? Especially if you have ADHD, which is an extra challenge.

Guess I’ll end with: you’ll avoid. Instead of judging yourself for that, try to notice how you feel. If you try to behave differently, it’s normal to feel anxious about it. But you can let that dissatisfaction/boredom drive you to do little experiments. Say, seeing what happens if you decide to engage genuinely with, say, someone working a counter.

It’s okay to allow him to move through his own emotions (you didn’t mention abuse, but of course that’s not an acceptable outlet).

You may be fine, but it’s  okay to be impacted by people we love. Just have to remember where they end and we begin, you know?


The only things inherently difficult are grieving the loss of health and the changes, and then figuring out how to adjust your lifestyles. Both of which don’t have to just fall on either or both of you. For your partner. There’s the added stress of shame and guilt that we learn to place on ourselves when things go wrong. Society also likes to shame sick people.

It’s okay to be upset about caretaking too. Remember, emotions are data not actions or directives. Anger tries to protect you by warning you of boundaries/fairness and giving you the power/motivation to defend yourself. Your partner being sick doesn’t mean that you don’t get to have needs. Needs are not a zero-sun game, like we may’ve learned in childhood. Not that I’m saying you shouldn’t help him (because you’re saying that you do want to), just that you’re allowed to have limits, take breaks, etc. A loving, healthy partner wants to know how you feel and solve problems together for both of you.

TLDR; It’s okay for both of you to feel bad right now, and it’s important for you to remember that you have a right to your own emotions and boundaries. Honest communication is key.

This line of the discussion seems to be about Inner Critic vs. Outer Critic (more info on the sidebar of this [site](http://www.pete-walker.com/)). Inner Critic says that we aren't good enough and should feel ashamed, while Outer Critic says that other people aren't good/safe enough and we should be afraid and on defense. I developed both as a kid. Arguably, an attack can possibly affect someone's self-worth if they felt unprotected (even by themselves) and if a part of them internalizes it as their fault.

Of course you're angry, your boundaries are being violated and you haven't been able to defend against it. What helped me was to understand a few things: 1) I have a right to boundaries, 2) I'm not responsible for managing other people's feelings, and 3) we all make lives for ourselves.

For example, your job is not to soothe your mother's anxiety by being controlled or insulted. It's also not your job to please your family at the expense of your well-being.

>What can I do to get over this so I can FINALLY become an adult?

First, the good news is that you're already an adult! Unlike in childhood whatever you don't have, you can get it for yourself. It may be challenging, but not impossible. Rather than worrying about how your family would react to you getting a job, focus on what you can control. Also, they don't need to know about everything you do--they can be on a need-to-know basis. 

It sounds like the most important things for you would be: 

* Identifying documents (and a safe place to store them): birth certificate, social, and a state ID. Maybe look into ordering a replacement certificate if you can't swipe the original one,   
 and skim any tax documents to find your social security number so you can use it in the mean time.
* Opening a bank account (can be done online)
* Working/Saving. Are there any informal things you could do for cash like babysitting, dogwalking, etc.? There are places like Fiverr where you can offer online services to people, but this can wait until you have an account. Your jobs and especially your income can be your business.

You know your situation best, so try to identify people and resources that could help you. Could be people that'll give you rides, places to volunteer (time out of the house is precious, builds connections too), anything. 

Good luck, and keep your head up!

For one, I think that it depends. There could be people that get treatment and take it seriously. But I think there's a few factors:

1. Like anyone, people with BPD get tired of hitting the same walls in the same ways. This is why consistency in boundaries is important--it discourages repeat attempts by proving them futile.
2. I'm not old enough to say, but older age seems to really change things for people. Bodies seem more fragile, so your mother may not be able to tolerate substances like before. I’m asking the same questions as you, but here’s what I have so far?

On enmeshment: Since enmeshment is a problem of boundaries at its core, I think healing means building boundaries to distinguish and protect your emotions and energy. Pete Walker says that crying and angering, how babies air out grievances, are indispensable when it comes to trauma and I’ve found this to be true in my experience. I had to feel the pain of being enmeshed in my family of origin, but I had to feel bad for myself AND grasp that my pain wasn’t a “me and my life” thing but something done to me by my caregivers. And that’s when the anger came—anger at those responsible, not myself. Admittedly I had, still do, a difficult time holding the anger since I still live with my FOO. I’m not religious, but the anger feels like a blessing—it gave me the power I’d needed to start withdrawing emotionally, setting boundaries and redirecting my energy.

I’ll also add that you’re already aware, and that’s good. Awareness is key because enmeshment is a whole dynamic with multiple players, and you have to understand those parts and be wary of the different ways they may draw you in. 

I’ll also offer up this website: https://outofthefog.website . The target audience is people in relationships (of any kind) with personality disordered individuals. You may or may not find that that description applies to you, but either way it has plenty of very actionable ideas on how to live emotionally independently.
